content: Balkan nephropathy, also known as Danubian endemic familial nephropathy (DEFN) or Balkan endemic nephropathy (BEN), is a chronic form of interstitial nephritis that is geographically restricted to certain rural areas in Bulgaria, the former Yugoslavia, and Romania. This condition is characterized by progressive kidney atrophy, often accompanied by urothelial tumors. It was first identified in the 1920s in small, isolated communities along the Danube River and its tributaries, in regions now part of Croatia, Bosnia, Serbia, Romania, and Bulgaria. A notable feature of this disease is its highly localized occurrence, with approximately ten small rural areas affected, without any apparent connection between these regions other than the presence of the illness. The first official description of Balkan nephropathy was published in 1956 by Dr. Yoto Tanchev, a Bulgarian nephrologist, and his team in the Bulgarian journal Savremena Medicina. Their research involved extensive screening of residents in villages near Vratsa, Bulgaria. Key clinical observations included the absence of high blood pressure, the presence of yellowish discoloration of the palms and soles (known as Tanchev's sign), early-onset hypochromic anemia, lack of proteinuria, and a slow progression to chronic kidney failure. The disease was initially named Vratsa nephritis. Later, similar conditions were reported in Yugoslavia and Romania, leading to the adoption of the term Balkan endemic nephropathy. Dr. Tanchev and his colleagues hypothesized that the disease was unique (sui generis) and initially suspected heavy metal intoxication as the cause, given that the affected villages relied on water from karst-type mountains near Vratsa. More recently, chronic exposure to dietary aristolochic acid has been proposed as a major risk factor for Balkan nephropathy. Aristolochic acid is derived from Aristolochia clematitis, a plant native to the endemic regions, whose seeds may contaminate wheat used for bread production. This hypothesis has gained support from research conducted by Dr. Arthur P. Grollman, a cancer biologist and director of the chemical biology lab at Stony Brook University, and Dr. Bojan Jelaković, an associate professor at the Zagreb University School of Medicine. Clinically, Balkan nephropathy is often asymptomatic in its early stages. It must be differentiated from other diseases that cause chronic kidney damage. The prevalence of the disease is estimated to be approximately 1 per 100,000 individuals worldwide, with cases primarily reported in the endemic regions. It affects men and women equally, with no racial predilection. The disease is more commonly observed in adults, with no cases reported in children. There is no specific treatment for Balkan nephropathy. Management is primarily supportive, focusing on slowing disease progression and addressing complications. Early clinical features may include anemia and mild renal dysfunction, but if left untreated, the disease can progress to chronic kidney failure and an increased risk of urothelial carcinoma. Prognosis varies, but many patients remain asymptomatic for extended periods before developing significant renal impairment.
